title: Adyen to Expand India Operations as Local Profits More Than Double
excerpt: The Dutch payments processor is betting on India's digital payments growth and rising cross-border commerce, with local headcount up tenfold since 2023 and pre-tax income at €3.18 million.
body:
• Adyen plans to expand its India operations and hire more employees, betting on the country's fast-growing digital payments market and rising cross-border commerce.
  • The company's pre-tax income from India more than doubled to €3.18 million in 2025, while its local headcount rose tenfold since 2023 to 120.
  • Asia-Pacific President Gary Yang called India a long-term growth market driven by multinationals entering the country and Indian businesses expanding abroad.
  • The Dutch processor has adapted its platform for India's payments landscape — UPI support, recurring mandates and data localisation — where rivals like Stripe and PayPal have stumbled.

Dutch payments processor Adyen plans to expand its India operations and hire more employees, betting on the country's fast-growing digital payments market and rising cross-border commerce. Asia-Pacific President Gary Yang, speaking to Reuters in an interview this week, described India as a long-term growth market for the Amsterdam-listed fintech — driven both by multinational clients entering the country and Indian businesses expanding overseas.

"We're continuing to hire and grow because we see significant opportunity in the market," Yang said, without disclosing India-specific hiring or growth targets.

Licences unlocked the growth path

Adyen's expansion follows its receipt of payment aggregator and cross-border licences from the Reserve Bank of India in 2024. Since then, its India business has scaled rapidly. Local employee count has risen tenfold since 2023 to 120 in the first half of this year, spread across Mumbai and Bengaluru. Pre-tax income from India more than doubled to €3.18 million ($3.5 million) in 2025 from €1.45 million a year earlier, annual reports showed.

That growth, while still modest against Adyen's global operations — which generated net income of €1.06 billion ($1.23 billion) in 2025 — signals the company's accelerating commercial traction in a market where global payments firms have historically struggled. Stripe scaled down its India operations in 2024 citing regulatory challenges, and PayPal exited domestic India payments in 2021, retreating to cross-border transactions.

Context and background

Adyen, one of the world's largest fintech firms, has operated in India for seven years. Its approach has been to localize deeply rather than force a global template: adapting its platform to India's regulatory and payments landscape, meeting data localisation requirements, supporting recurring payment mandates, and building UPI capabilities.

"There is no succeeding in India without UPI," Yang told Reuters. India's Unified Payments Interface is one of the largest instant payments networks in the world, processing billions of transactions every month — and it is a layer that global processors have repeatedly underestimated.

The company is also positioning itself for the rise of AI-powered "agentic commerce," in which software agents search for products and complete purchases on behalf of consumers. Reuters reported last week that the National Payments Corporation of India is preparing a framework that would let AI agents make small digital payments without seeking approval for every transaction.

Impact and analysis

Adyen's two-sided bet is notable. On one side, it is working with multinational clients — including Uber, Microsoft and Adobe — that are expanding their Indian payments operations. On the other, it is helping Indian clients such as travel platform Oyo take payments abroad. That twin engine — inbound and outbound — is where the cross-border opportunity lies.

The company told Mint it plans to grow its local product, commercial and operations teams. "We think that to win in India, we want to be here for the long term. We've been here for seven years already. We're going to continue to invest in India because we believe that's what it takes to really understand the local business, understand the local customer, and build the right product," Yang said. He added that India ranks among the company's top three global priorities.

The doubling of pre-tax income is the clearest evidence yet that the licensing bet is paying off. For global fintech investors, Adyen's India trajectory is becoming a counter-example to the broader narrative that India's payments market is impenetrable for foreign players — at least for those willing to build for UPI, localize data, and play the long game.

What's next

The company gave no specific hiring numbers or revenue targets for India. But with licences in hand, a growing client roster on both sides of the border, and agentic commerce on the horizon, Adyen's next phase in India will be about scaling headcount and product depth. Analysts will be watching whether the tenfold hiring growth since 2023 continues — and whether local profits keep doubling alongside it.
